summary: On-chain npm supply-chain risk assessment. Validators agree on a 16-ordinal feature vector; every score is integer arithmetic over it.

data_sources.rejected: https://registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search returns npms.io's own quality/popularity/maintenance scores. Deliberately unused: consuming it would make PackageGuard a cache of somebody else's score.

corpus_totals.what_this_shows: Average maintenance is 37 against security 80 and maturity 89. npm's problem is not that packages are badly built, it is that they stop being looked after - which is why maintenance carries the same 25% weight as popularity.

determinism_result.what_this_shows: Two independent validator rounds, minutes apart. All 15 PARSED ordinals identical; the single model-derived ordinal (desc) moved one rung. The 3-point model bound plus step-5 quantization absorbed it entirely and the published score did not move. Within each round every validator agreed - _agrees has no tolerance, so the round could not have committed otherwise.
determinism_result.caveat: The two deployments differ by one commit, a licence-prefix-matching tightening that cannot affect an MIT package, so lic is 2 under both.

composability_result.consumer: PackageConsumer.add_dependency goes through PackageGuard.require_safe, which REVERTS rather than returning false.

refused.esbuild: REVERT: carries banned flag(s) INSTALL_SCRIPTS; it scores 80 but the policy is not about the score alone
refused.flatmap-stream: REVERT: scores 30 (HIGH_RISK), below the required 50; flags: NO_LICENSE,ABANDONED,SINGLE_MAINTAINER,PRERELEASE,LOW_ADOPTION,NO_RECENT_RELEASE
refused.lodash: REVERT: no scan on record for lodash

composability_result.degradation: preview_dependency on the same unscanned package returns {allowed:false, verdict:'BLOCK', reason:'never scanned; call PackageGuard.request_scan'} instead of reverting, so a UI can explain rather than fail.
composability_result.why_esbuild_matters: esbuild scores 80 and is SAFE - healthy and actively maintained - and the CI gate refuses it anyway for running a postinstall. The oracle says how well kept a package is; whether that is acceptable is the consumer's decision, and they are separate contracts for exactly that reason.

verify_result.note: verify_risk recomputed the record from `evidence` alone - five scores, level, badge, confidence, every flag and the content hash - and matched.

cross_network_result.same_hash_across_networks: Produced independently on Studionet (0x1F3f51d9927490543519d6C61b9B544bf5caA7FB) and Bradbury (0x4f35Fd3D93bDb8446C3ccf715B684222D93BB8fE) by DIFFERENT VALIDATOR SETS on different networks.
cross_network_result.what_this_shows: All sixteen ordinals matched, the model-derived `desc` included, so the FNV digest over (package name + vector) is the same string on both chains. The artifact is also byte-identical across the two deployments, sha256 56fd5144... - so this is one program, run by two independent validator sets, agreeing exactly.
cross_network_result.the_honest_caveat: The model is not guaranteed to agree across rounds. An earlier Studionet deployment produced desc=1 for the same package and hence a different hash (162:af56133f1fdf6976) - while `overall` stayed 85, because the model's 3-point bound plus step-5 quantization absorbed the difference. Determinism is enforced WITHIN a round with no tolerance; across rounds the fifteen parsed ordinals are stable and the one model ordinal is bounded.
